newsitem.title: USA: Clinton said to withdraw Lake's nomination for CIA.
newsitem.headline: Clinton said to withdraw Lake's nomination for CIA.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday reluctantly agreed to pull the nomination of Anthony Lake, one of his closest advisers, to be CIA director, administration sources said.

Lake, Clinton's first-term national security adviser, was frustrated by the bitter partisan climate holding up his confirmation and urged Clinton to withdraw his name in a White House meeting on Monday, one sources said.
Lake followed up the meeting with an "eloquent" letter explaining his reasons for stepping aside, the source said.

The decision followed three days of tough confirmation hearings last week, in which members of the Senate Intelligence Committee questioned Lake's integrity, management skills and fitness to head the Central Intelligence Agency.

But it came a surprise to many who had predicted Lake's eventual confirmation and praised his performance in last week's often testy Senate hearings. The panel was due to resume hearings on Lake's nomination on Tuesday.

Lake's sudden withdrawal also marked a setback for Clinton, who had praised Lake as one of the central architects of U.S. policies that stabilized crises in Bosnia and Haiti and broadened the thaw in U.S. relations with Russia.
Lake is one of the final members of Clinton's second-term team awaiting Senate confirmation, and most others have sailed through their confirmation hearings.

"He met with the president today and the president very reluctantly, and after trying to convince Tony to fight it, accepted his personal judgment that he ought to withdraw his nomination," said the source, who asked not to be identified.

Asked why Lake had decided to withdraw himself from consideration for the CIA post, he cited Lake's "belief that the committee would delay endlessly ... and that the president would be deprived of a director of central intelligence."
One administration source said Lake had become convinced the committee would "nibble him to death rather than deal with the nomination straight-up anytime soon."
Lake had proposed withdrawing his name before last week's confirmation hearings, but had been dissuaded at that point, the source said.

In a letter explaining his withdrawal, Lake called the confirmation process "nasty and brutish without being short," and said that "Washington has gone haywire" in partisanship, the Washington Post and ABC Radio reported.
No comment was immediately available from the White House.

Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, issued a statement late on Monday saying, "This nomination has been wrought with controversy from the beginning. Although I found Mr. Lake to be intelligent and amicable, I continue to have strong reservations about his fitness to be the director of central intelligence."
The ranking Democrat on the panel, Sen. Bob Kerrey, said he regretted the circumstances surrounding Lake's withdrawal and called Lake's treatment by the panel "unfair."

Lake would have been Clinton's third CIA director and the fifth in six years. The agency has been rocked by treason in its ranks, frequent changes in leadership and scandals in Guatemala and elsewhere.

Lake has been dogged by questions about why his staff did not inform him of an FBI briefing on an alleged Chinese plan to influene U.S. elections, and his decision to keep Congrss in the dark about tacit U.S. approval of Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Muslims in 1994.
He was expected to face more grilling about a report that a controversial oil man visited Clinton at the White House despite objections by Lake's National Security Council.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry earlier confirmed the "bare bones" of a Wall Street Journal report that Lebanese-born international oil man and Democratic donor Roger Tamraz visited Clinton in the White House four times despite objections raised about him by an NSC official in 1995.

In last week's hearings, Lake reiterated that he should have been alerted about the FBI's concerns over any Chinese plan to steer funds secretly to candidates for federal office. "There appears to have been some kind of a breakdown here," he said of the failure to pass the alert up the line to him.
But he denied it was indicative of any systematic failure of his own to properly manage the 151-member council staff.
